articles.title: Australian universities consider job and course cuts amid financial pressures; what Indian students should check before choosing a campus
articles.summary: Indian students planning to study in Australia may need to look beyond university rankings and course fees when choosing an institution, as several
articles.body: Indian students planning to study in Australia may need to look beyond university rankings and course fees when choosing an institution, as several universities in Victoria are considering staff reductions and reviewing academic programmes amid mounting financial pressures. The developments have raised questions about the financial sustainability of universities and the possible implications for teaching, student support and course availability.The University of Melbourne has identified around 179 positions that could be affected by restructuring, Deakin University is preparing voluntary redundancy measures, and Federation University is reviewing arts and humanities subjects with low enrolments. The developments, reported by Times Higher Education (THE) on November 17, come amid concerns that declining international student numbers, rising operating costs and uncertainty over government policy are putting additional pressure on Australia's higher education sector.University of Melbourne identifies 179 positions for possible cutsThe University of Melbourne has put forward eight restructuring proposals that could affect approximately 179 positions across its workforce of around 13,800 employees. Some of the positions are already vacant.According to Times Higher Education, the roles under consideration are largely in non-academic areas, including alumni relations, biomedicine, financial planning, philanthropy and technology.The university said it had introduced measures to reduce discretionary spending and unnecessary travel. It also cited changes affecting international students as a source of considerable financial pressure on universities across Australia.Deakin University prepares voluntary redundancy measuresDeakin University is preparing voluntary redundancies as it responds to a projected revenue decline of between A$200 million and A$250 million by 2029.Acting vice-chancellor Susan Elliott told staff that the university would provide an update on its redundancy proposal on November 19. She described the measures as an early response to the institution's financial outlook.According to THE, Elliott said international student numbers had fallen across the university sector and described the change as structural rather than temporary. Deakin has also tightened recruitment, requiring approval for appointments to new or vacant non-academic positions.Federation University reviews arts and humanities coursesFederation University is reviewing arts and humanities subjects with particularly low enrolments as it attempts to manage operating costs.The university has attributed some of its financial difficulties to government underfunding and restrictions on new international students. It has also pointed to the impact of the Job-ready Graduates policy, which increased student contributions for several arts and humanities degrees.The National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU) has called on the university to rule out further cuts. Federation University, however, has clarified that it is not planning a major course purge and is reviewing subjects with very low enrolments.Australian commission chief warns of risks to researchThe developments come as Australian Tertiary Education Commission chief commissioner Barney Glover warns that uncertainty surrounding international education could affect universities' teaching and research capabilities.Speaking at the University of Sydney's 2026 Bradley Oration, Glover called for more predictable government policies, particularly regarding student visa processing and international education settings.As quoted by Times Higher Education, Glover said: "Volatility impacts our universities almost existentially." He also warned that declining international student revenue could weaken universities' ability to support research activities.What Indian students should check before choosing an Australian universityFor Indian students considering Australia, the developments do not mean that the affected universities have stopped admitting international students or that their degrees are no longer recognised. However, prospective applicants should pay attention to institutional changes before accepting an offer.Students should check:• Course availability: Confirm that the chosen programme will run for the intended intake and has not been affected by a course review.• Teaching arrangements: Ask whether restructuring could affect faculty availability, academic supervision or course delivery.• Student support: Check the availability of international student services, career guidance and academic assistance.• Campus facilities: Seek clarity on any planned changes to campus operations and student services.• University updates: Follow official announcements about restructuring, course reviews and changes to academic departments.The developments underline the importance of assessing a university's academic offering, financial position and student support arrangements alongside its rankings and reputation. For students making a significant financial commitment to overseas education, understanding how an institution is responding to financial pressures is an important part of choosing the right campus.Get the latest Education News and Live updates. articles.title: Conmoción en los hipódromos: encuentran un famoso caballo de carreras muerto en un contenedor
articles.summary: El mundo de las carreras de caballos ha quedado conmocionado tras el hallazgo, en un contenedor de residuos, de un caballo que participó en la Melbourne Cup y que murió después de sufrir un cólico grave.
articles.body: El mundo de las carreras de caballos ha quedado conmocionado tras el hallazgo, en un contenedor de residuos, de un caballo que participó en la Melbourne Cup y que murió después de sufrir un cólico grave. El cadáver de 'So You Are' fue hallado entre los desechos generales en las instalaciones de Cleanaway en Lucas Heights (Sídney). "Estoy en el vertedero. ¡Han tirado un caballo en el puto contenedor. ¿Me estás tomando el pelo? Esto no puede ser normal. ¿Alguien sabe si es legal? Me da un asco tremendo».", comentó Gregg Jowett, el trabajador de la construcción que, tras en encontrar el cadáver del caballo y dar la voz de alarma, denunció la situación en un vídeo que publicó en Facebook. Tras enterarse de la existencia de las imágenes, Bjorn Baker, entrenador de So You Are, y el resto de las personas vinculadas al caballo expresaron su consternación en un comunicado. "Al igual que todos los que han visto las imágenes, me siento profundamente consternado por la forma en que se trataron los restos de So You Are. Era un caballo muy querido y merecía ser tratado con dignidad y respeto tras su muerte", compartió Baker. El caballo había sido trasladado de urgencia a la clínica REC Equine Specialists, en Randwick, para someterse a una cirugía de emergencia después de sufrir un cólico. Los veterinarios le practicaron la eutanasia al caballo tras constatar que no era posible salvarlo. "REC Equine Specialists expresa su más sentido pésame a los propietarios, al entrenador y a las personas vinculadas a So You Are, y pide disculpas sin reservas por la angustia causada por las imágenes difundidas hoy en las redes sociales. El lunes 16 de noviembre, So You Are fue trasladado a nuestro hospital para recibir tratamiento de urgencia por un cólico grave. A pesar de los denodados esfuerzos de nuestro equipo veterinario, no fue posible salvarlo, por lo que se le practicó la eutanasia de forma humanitaria bajo anestesia. Tras su fallecimiento, So You Are fue recogido por nuestro proveedor de servicios externo y trasladado a un vertedero autorizado. Debería haber sido enterrado de manera pronta y respetuosa" declaró Jonathan Lumsden a news.com.au.

articles.title: Education Department touts changes made to student loans, K-12 investments after a year of interagency agreements
articles.summary: The Education Department on Wednesday touted changes to major policies such as student loans and education funding that have come as a result of its 14 interagency agreements. Over the past year, the Department of Education has made agreements with the Treasury Department, State Department and others to move some its responsibilities and programs out…
articles.body:
The Education Department on Wednesday touted changes to major policies such as student loans and education funding that have come as a result of its 14 interagency agreements.

Over the past year, the Department of Education has made agreements with the Treasury Department, State Department and others to move some its responsibilities and programs out of its purview as President Trump seeks to wind down the entire department.

The announcement provides fresh details of what those agreements have produced, such as the Treasury and Education Department working together to create the Defaulted Loans Support Center.

The center gives resources to defaulted borrowers to get back into good standing on their payments, with 89 percent of early user feedback saying the new rehabilitation process was easy, according to the department.

“For too long, Washington measured success by how many rules it wrote rather than how well students were doing,” Secretary of Education Linda McMahon said. “By working together across six federal departments this past year, we have delivered meaningful wins for families — cutting through the red tape that stands in the way of learning, connecting classrooms to careers, and bolstering enforcement of federal law. Congress now has an opportunity to cement these reforms into law and help return education decisions where they belong: with parents, teachers, and local communities.”

The partnership with the Department of Labor, the Trump administration said, led to $425 million in investments “to boost literacy, expand charter school access, support career-connected learning, strengthen teacher preparation, bolster American History and Civics education, and modernize state academic assessments.”

The interagency agreements have come under fire from opponents who call them confusing and say they do not actually reduce the red tape the administration is aiming to trim.

In line with Trump and McMahon’s stated goal to abolish the department, the agency has taken drastic steps, such as firing half of its workforce.

But to completely shut the doors of the Education Department would take an act of Congress, an idea that stands no chance after Democrats’ victories in this month’s midterm elections.

Opponents argue the department began the interagency agreements as a way to circumvent that roadblock and further weaken itself.

Democrats have promised investigations into the agreements after they retake the House and Senate, with mounting concerns over issues such as the number of unresolved civil rights investigations.

In the Wednesday announcement, the Education Department said the Office of Civil Rights partnership with the Department of Justice has “streamlined the complaint resolution process” and has created more effective enforcement.

It also highlighted the partnership with the Department of Health and Human Services and emphasized that the Education Department is still the head of oversight for programs with students with disabilities and all funding allocations reached states on time.

The two agencies also gave 40 new grants totaling $71 million to low-income college parents to access child care.

“President Trump and Secretary McMahon are cutting red tape and putting families first,” said Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “HHS is helping strengthen services for students with disabilities, expand affordable child care for parents earning degrees, and support early learning. We’re making federal agencies work together to deliver for American families.”

Other progress the Education Department highlighted included strengthening tribal relations, grants to employment-focused programs and protecting student privacy.

articles.title: Miguel, joven viviendo en Australia: "Llevo dos meses y ya he dejado tres trabajos"
articles.standfirst: El creador de contenido ha contado su experiencia a través de sus redes sociales
articles.summary: El creador de contenido ha contado su experiencia a través de sus redes sociales
articles.body: Australia se ha convertido en uno de los destinos preferidos por los jóvenes para buscar las oportunidades que no encuentran en sus países de origen. Un ejemplo de ello es Miguel, un joven de 23 años que nació en Cali, Colombia. “Llevo dos meses en Australia y ya he dejado tres trabajos”, comenzaba contando en sus redes sociales, asegurando que allí dejar y encontrar un empleo es mucho más sencillo; de hecho, es habitual. “Después de aterrizar en Gold Coast y haber visto más de 35 casas hasta que alguna me aceptara, he dejado mis tres trabajos para empezar de cero. Te contaré cómo es vivir en una de las mejores ciudades de Australia, qué planes hacer, cómo buscar trabajo y sobre todo, cómo es vivir esta gran aventura”, explicaba el creador de contenido, que tiene claro que allí le espera una nueva vida. Australia se ha consolidado como uno de los principales polos de atracción para jóvenes de todo el mundo, especialmente de Latinoamérica y Europa, gracias a su alta calidad de vida, salarios competitivos y flexibilidad para estudiar y trabajar. Este fenómeno responde tanto a la búsqueda de estabilidad económica como a las políticas migratorias del país para cubrir la escasez de mano de obra. El país cuenta con uno de los salarios mínimos por hora más altos a nivel global, lo que permite a los recién llegados cubrir sus gastos de manutención e incluso ahorrar trabajando a tiempo parcial. Además, sectores como la hostelería, la construcción, el turismo, la agricultura y los servicios de cuidado presentan una oferta constante de empleo que no requiere un dominio perfecto del inglés desde el primer día. Los datos más recientes del Gobierno australiano muestran un flujo histórico de más de un millón de jóvenes internacionales, sumando estudiantes y viajeros con visados de trabajo y vacaciones entre 2025 y 2026. Esta cifra incluye un récord de 323.077 visados Working Holiday concedidos y 738.694 estudiantes extranjeros activos en el país.

articles.title: McDonald's sex abuse: 'They were waiting for the younger girls to turn 18'
articles.summary: A former McDonald's worker calls on the firm to “change the way they treat younger employees” as a judge rules a legal case against the chain can go ahead.
articles.body:
A former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has called on the firm to “change the way they treat younger employees”.

Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023, also told BBC News she saw older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers, and talking about wanting to sleep with them when they turned 18.

Hope is one of hundreds of workers bringing a discrimination claim against McDonald's. This week, a judge ruled against McDonald's attempt to have their claims struck out, a move that Hope welcomed.

McDonald's said: "Ensuring a safe, respectful and inclusive working environment across our restaurants and offices remains a fundamental priority."

The latest developments come after a BBC investigation in 2023 which heard that workers, some as young as 17, were being groped and harassed.

Last year, McDonald's staff told us they still faced sexual abuse and harassment.

Hope, who is now 22, says that her branch of McDonalds had a very sexualised, "toxic" environment.

She spoke of a time a manager came up behind her and put his hands on her shoulders. From then on, whenever she saw him coming over, she says she "moved quick" to get away from him.

"I got the hell out of there," she says.

Another time, she says a manager failed to protect her when she says she was being sexualised and objectified by two customers on a night shift.

Hope says she told the manager what was happening, but he told her to "just suck it up and deal with it".

Her main concern, however, was for the younger teenagers, who she says weren't being looked after.

"You could tell there were other staff members waiting for their 18th birthdays. That sort of like toxic culture where it's like, 'Oh, you know, it's not illegal now.' It was that feeling from quite a few of them," she says.

"And why would you? That is literally a child still."

Hundreds of current and former McDonald's employees are bringing a discrimination claim against the firm.

The fast-food chain had attempted to have the complaints thrown out but this week at the London Central Employment Tribunal, Judge Glennie ruled that 450 cases can go ahead and they are now expected to be heard at the Employment Tribunal in April.

The BBC understands that these relate to indirect discrimination, not sexual harassment.

Hope told us she was not taking part in the legal case for money, saying they didn't know if they were going to get anything.

Instead, she said it was to try and "change the way they treat younger employees".

"It's going to change the way they treat allegations. It's going to shake up the whole internal process and make life easier for the kids who are now having their first jobs. And it's going to make it a lot safer, I think, as well. And that's something you can't put a price on, the safety of the young these days.''

She also accused McDonald's of trying to "delay the inevitable" by attempting to have the claims thrown out.

"And the judge quite rightly looked at them and said: 'No. We're not going to do that.'"

The claims were presented by law firm Leigh Day, which is acting for the current and former employees.

The claims focus on the vulnerability of young or female workers in the workplace and follow allegations of widespread harassment and discrimination across McDonald's restaurants in the UK.

Leigh Day partner Kiran Daurka told the BBC: "We're really delighted that the judge has found that these claims can go forward to a full hearing. It's really important for access to justice that these cases are heard."

A McDonald's spokesperson said they could not comment on the specifics of ongoing legal proceedings.

In a statement, they said the company had "embedded an extensive set of robust and far-reaching initiatives" as part of its "steadfast commitment" to its staff, adding that this work continues.

"Any form of harassment, discrimination or inappropriate behaviour is unacceptable and has no place in our restaurants or offices. We are confident that with the guidance and partnership of external experts, we and our franchisees have industry leading safeguarding measures in place," the spokesperson added.
